# Evaluation {#sec-sys-eval}

Evaluation is how you decide whether a model is good enough to ship and
whether a change helped. This chapter explains how evaluation practice got
the shape it has: why offline metrics drift from product outcomes, why a
benchmark decays as a signal, and what an evaluation number actually
estimates. By the end a reader can attach a confidence interval to a result
and reason about when a measured difference is real.

## Problem

You need a number that predicts product quality, is cheap enough to run on
every change, and does not quietly mislead. The constraints are noise, cost,
validity, and contamination.

## Design

A reproducible harness with versioned datasets, prompts, and graders;
automated and model-graded scoring calibrated against humans; and online
experiments for the outcomes offline metrics cannot see.

## Evolution

From fixed academic benchmarks, to held-out task suites, to model-as-judge
evaluation, to continuous online experimentation. Trace why each was forced
by the failure of the one before it, including benchmark contamination.

## Trade-offs

Automated scoring is cheap but biased. Human evaluation is trustworthy but
slow and costly. Online tests measure the real outcome but risk users.
Where each is the right tool.

## In practice

Deterministic runs, continuous evaluation in CI, guardrail metrics, drift
detection, and catching regressions before users do.

## Foundations

What the numbers mean. A score as a sample statistic, confidence intervals
and significance, construct validity, contamination as signal decay, and
online tests as causal inference.

$$
\widehat{\text{acc}} \pm z \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\text{acc}}(1 - \widehat{\text{acc}})}{n}}
$$
